messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The night the men came for him, Marcin had been walking home from a late shift at the processing plant, a short cut through an alley he had taken a hundred times. They were three, maybe four—he could never be sure afterwards—and they had a crowbar and a length of pipe. What he remembered most vividly, what his body remembered when it would not let him forget, was the sensation of being forced to his knees on the cold, wet asphalt, the pipe pressed hard into the small of his back, and the sound of a baby crying from a window somewhere above them. He did not know whose baby it was, but that thin, insistent wail had cut through the grunts and the blows, and it had become the soundtrack to the half-hour that followed. The men had beaten him systematically, methodically, asking questions he could not answer, and when they were finished, they left him curled on the ground with a fractured rib, a shattered collarbone, and a ringing in his ears that took days to fade. The physical pain had been immense, but it was the rage that had surprised him most—a hot, blinding fury that had risen in his chest even as they worked, a fury that had no outlet, that just sat there, seething, waiting.

Now, at twenty-six, Marcin is a fisherman, working out of a small port town on the New England coast. He chose the job because it keeps him on open water, where there is nothing behind him but the horizon and he can see every approach. On the boat, with his back to the wheelhouse and the vast Atlantic in front of him, he feels something close to safe. The trouble starts when he comes ashore. A crowded bus, for instance, is unbearable. The press of bodies, the lack of exits, the way passengers stand behind him—it sends a jolt of cold recognition through his spine, and before he knows it, his body has locked into that familiar position: knees bent, head down, shoulders braced for impact. The memory floods back not as a thought but as a physical fact. He feels the pipe against his vertebrae again, the grinding of his collarbone, and the rage returns, hot and useless, making his hands tremble. That rage, in turn, sharpens his senses to a razor edge. He scans the bus for anything that could be used as a weapon—a fire extinguisher, a glass bottle, the sharp edge of a seat frame—and he listens, not to the chatter of passengers, but for the specific quality of sound that might mean someone is moving toward him. He has come to believe that if he is not vigilant, if he does not monitor every threat, he will be caught off guard again. And that hypervigilance, that constant scanning and listening, makes the bus ride a gauntlet of triggers. Every sudden stop, every raised voice, every crying baby—and babies are the worst, because that sound is a direct line back to the alley—each one snaps him into a fresh flash of memory, a fresh wave of physical pain in his ribs and collarbone, a fresh surge of that helpless, boiling rage.

The cycle has cost him. He no longer visits his sister, because she has a six-month-old and the sound of the baby crying sends him pacing out of the house without a word. His wife, Anna, has learned to warn him before they go anywhere, to check if the bus will be crowded, to sit with her back to the wall in restaurants so he can face the door. She does this without complaint, but Marcin knows she is tired. He sees it in the way she hesitates before suggesting an evening out. What finally brought him to the clinic was a moment on the boat last week. A crewmate had clapped him on the shoulder from behind, joking, and Marcin had spun around with his fist raised, his whole body locked in that old position, the rage so close to the surface that it frightened him. He had not hit the man, but he had seen the fear in his eyes, and he had known, then, that something had to change. He is afraid of what he might do if the cycle tightens any further, but he is also afraid of what it would mean to let go of the vigilance—to stop watching, to stop listening, to trust that no one is coming for him.
